title: Students Are Customers
author: Dempsey, Patrick
summary: In the concluding installment of his airline-education series, Patrick Dempsey applies the Rule of Reciprocity to higher education's student motivation crisis: students are increasingly disengaged because the educational system withdraws -- through requirements, deadlines, and policies -- before making any deposits. Airlines have mastered the art of making an inherently uncomfortable experience survivable through choreographed reciprocity (greetings, maps, snacks, narration during turbulence), and education needs to learn the same lesson. Dempsey invokes Alex Hormozi's 'give, give, give, ask' principle and Gottman's 5:1 positive-to-negative interaction ratio to argue that course design failure is fundamentally about inverted deposit-withdrawal ratios, not about student laziness or surveillance gaps. The article's honest acknowledgment that no one can be certain which cognitive skills will matter in five to twenty years makes the reciprocity argument more urgent: if teachers cannot be sure the content is essential, the relational investment must be non-negotiable. AI has accelerated the credibility problem: students can now see in real time that AI can do the assigned work, so the only remaining argument for compliance is relational, not instrumental. The article closes by noting that traditional higher ed's structural props -- legacy prestige, credential requirements, family conviction in degrees -- are eroding, and the underlying challenge of student belief is arriving faster than institutions can adapt.
points: Students disengage not because content is too hard but because the educational system withdraws first -- requirements, deadlines, and policies before any deposits; the trust ratio is reversed from what human relationships require.

The Hormozi 'give, give, give, ask' model maps cleanly onto course design: front-loading value earns the right to make demands, whereas opening with a syllabus full of requirements signals that the relationship is extractive from the start.

Gottman's 5:1 ratio means negative experiences in a course carry disproportionate emotional weight -- bad assignments, arbitrary policies, and delayed feedback must be offset by five positive interactions to maintain the learning relationship.

AI has made the credibility problem acute: students can now see in real time that AI can do the assigned work, so the only remaining argument for student compliance is relational -- the course must earn their trust before it can ask for effort.

Generosity in course design is not surrender to a consumer model; it is the foundational model of human relationships -- one that airlines have encoded systematically and education has mostly ignored.
quotes: Students don't believe us anymore. They can see that AI can do the thing we're asking them to do. While they might think the degree has value, the work we are asking them to complete to get there lacks all credibility.

The idea is that you earn the right to make a request by making deposits first. The idea is that you deliver so much value that the person who receives it feels almost obligated to reciprocate. Now, think about your course, do you do that???

We open with a syllabus full of requirements, deadlines, and consequences... Then, once the course does begin, what do we do? We spend the entire semester asking. This assignment. This due date. This policy. There is no give before the take.
Negative experiences are expensive. If a learning experience takes from students repeatedly without giving enough back, the relationship to you and the course cannot but degrade.

Every move in the Aviation Behavioral Engineering framework is, at its core, a deposit. The greeting, the vent, the map, the snack, the calm voice during turbulence... none of it removes the discomfort. But all of it is the system giving something back before it asks for more compliance.
Generosity is not surrender to the 'consumer model' of education, it is the foundational model of human relationships.
The question this article asks is simply: Are you giving anything to them first?
